posts.title: How I rescue a stalled Laravel codebase in the first week
posts.excerpt: The exact five-day routine I run when a client hands me a half-finished app, a missing developer and a launch date that won't move.

body.text: Most of the projects I take on now don't start from a blank repo. They start with a message like: "Our developer stopped replying, the app is 70% done, and we've already told customers it launches next month."

The instinct is to rewrite. It's almost always the wrong call. A rewrite throws away months of decisions you've already paid for and resets the clock to zero. Instead, I spend the first week finding out exactly what's there and making it safe to change.
Day 1 - Get it running on my machine

Before I read a single controller, I try to boot the app locally. This alone tells me a lot: missing env variables, a database that only exists on the old developer's laptop, packages pinned to versions that no longer install.

composer install
cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
php artisan migrate --seed
php artisan test
If any of those four commands fails, that's my first finding - and usually the first fix.

I walk every route the user can reach and note what works, what errors and what's half-built. I read the migrations to understand the data model, then check the payment and auth flows first - those are where bugs cost real money.

The client gets a short written report: what's solid, what's broken, what's missing, and a prioritised list to get to launch. Plain English, no jargon. This is the document that turns "I hope this works" into a plan with dates.
A stalled project rarely needs a rewrite. It needs someone to read the code, tell the truth about it and start shipping.
I add error tracking, fix the crashes found on day two, and write a handful of tests around the most important flows - sign-up, checkout, the core feature. Now I can change code without fear.
Day 5 - Ship something the client can see
By Friday there's a staging link and a short demo. Even if it's only a fixed checkout and a working admin login, momentum matters. From here it's weekly demos until launch.
If your project is stuck somewhere between "almost done" and "never launched", that first week is usually what gets it moving again.
